title: Regulatory Authority and Legal Basis for Customs Exemptions
summary: The Second Schedule has evolved from a general reference point for tax exemptions under the 1969 Customs Act to a specific, multi-faceted legal anchor under the Customs Act, 2023. It now serves as a primary mechanism for defining industrial warehouse privileges, duty-free import conditions, and specific regulatory exemptions for export-oriented industries.

evolution.legal_basis: Shifted from Customs Act 1969 to Customs Act 2023.
evolution.scope: Expanded from energy sector exemptions to comprehensive industrial warehouse and export-oriented regulatory frameworks.
evolution.structure: Moved from general schedule references to specific itemized serial numbers (e.g., 7, 11, 32, 35).

timeline.change: Initial reference to Second Schedule under the 1969 Customs Act for energy sector exemptions.
Integration of Second Schedule with Supplementary Duty (SD) adjustments and Margin of Preference calculations.
Formal transition to Customs Act, 2023, linking specific serial numbers of the Second Schedule to industrial warehouse and duty-free import regulations.
Refinement of export-oriented industrial warehouse procedures linked to specific clauses of the Second Schedule.

Customs Act 1969: Section 19(1) of this Act empowers the Government to provide exemptions from customs duties for specific goods imported under defined conditions.
Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty A: Section 126(1) of this Act authorizes the government to grant exemptions from value-added tax and supplementary duty in the public interest.
Oil and Gas Exploration and Production E: This order provides customs duty, value-added tax, and supplementary duty exemptions for the import of machinery and equipment intended for oil and gas exploration and production.
The exemption applies to imports by specific state-owned entities under the Bangladesh Oil, Gas and Mineral Corporation (Petrobangla) and companies operating under Production Sharing Contracts.

Equipment may be imported permanently for authorized operational use or temporarily under a re-export condition, subject to compliance with specific certification, reporting, and disposal requirements.
Items listed in the second schedule that are not directly involved in exploration and production activities are excluded from these duty and tax concessions.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is the authority responsible for overseeing the implementation of these exemptions and must be consulted by the government for such orders.

Importers must provide regular progress and inventory reports to the Board, and prior approval is required for the import of specific vehicles and any potential sale or transfer of duty-exempted goods.
Customs Authority: Customs authorities manage the clearance of imported equipment, receive required certifications and affidavits from importers, and oversee the disposal of damaged or non-functional equipment.
In cases of unauthorized use of duty-exempted goods, the Customs Authority is empowered to take necessary legal action against the importer.

Customs Act 2023: Section 263 of the Customs Act 2023, read in conjunction with specific sections of its sixteenth chapter and second schedule, serves as the legal basis for exercising the government's power to amend existing warehouse procedures.
Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty A: Section 135 of this Act provides the legislative authority, alongside the Customs Act, for the government to implement changes to warehouse operating procedures for export-oriented industries.
National Board of Revenue: The government is required to consult with the National Board of Revenue when exercising its powers to amend industrial warehouse rules.
Export-Oriented Industries (Bonded Wareh: These rules govern the temporary import and warehouse operations for direct and deemed export-oriented industries, excluding the garment sector.

Rule 10(2) of these rules is amended to refine the documentary requirements for approving the Utilization Permission (UP), specifically mandating a direct connection between the master financial instruments and the back-to-back letters of credit.

Customs Act 2023: This act provides the legal authority under sections 263 and specific serials of the second schedule for amending customs-related procedures.
The National Board of Revenue exercises its regulatory powers granted by this act to reform industrial manufacturing operations.
Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty A: Section 135 of this act serves as an enabling provision for the amendments made to the warehouse operations and manufacturing rules.
Direct Export-Oriented Garment Industry: This instrument is amended to adjust export performance requirements, increase operational timelines, and refine procedures for contract manufacturing.
The amendments modify sub-rules regarding material transfers, record keeping for contract production, annual audit requirements, sub-contract payments, and timelines for procedural compliance.
National Board of Revenue: The board exercises its authority to amend warehouse and export-oriented industry rules in consultation with relevant stakeholders.
The board issues specific directives regarding Value Added Tax exemptions for sub-contracting payments made in local currency.
Business Identification Number: This identification number is a mandatory record-keeping requirement for contract manufacturing agreements.
Sub-contracting permissions are strictly prohibited if an institution's business identification number is currently suspended.
Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Transact: These guidelines must be strictly followed when verifying that payments for contract manufacturing agreements are settled in foreign currency during annual audits.

Customs Act 2023: Section 12 and the Second Schedule of this Act provide the legal authority for granting duty-free import privileges for raw materials under specific industrial conditions.
Duty-Free Import: Duty-free import of raw materials is permitted specifically for licensed shipbuilding or dredger manufacturing industrial units. This benefit applies to materials procured against local supply orders that are payable in foreign currency through international tenders.
